text.en: Rani is a curious girl who asks many questions. One morning her brother Pratik shouts that India is on the Moon. The children visit Nandini Aunty, a scientist, who explains how a rocket carried Chandrayaan to the Moon. In this chapter you will read the story, learn the words curious and scientist, use a and an correctly, form words with sk, sw, sp and st, and learn the days of the week with their positions.

Rani lived in a village and was very curious. She asked many questions to her family, teachers and friends. She asked why the sky is blue and where the Sun goes at night. One evening she heard her mother singing about Chanda Mama and asked how far the Moon is. Her mother said it is very far in the sky, and Rani fell asleep thinking about the Moon.
Next morning her brother Pratik shouted in excitement, pointing at the TV, Look Rani, India is on the Moon. On the TV Rani saw photos of machines on the Moon and heard people talking about the landing. She was confused and asked how Chandrayaan reached the Moon. Pratik said his friend Vivaan's mother, Nandini Aunty, is a scientist, so they went to visit her.
Rani and Pratik saw many models and photographs of rockets in Vivaan's house. Nandini Aunty offered sharbat and asked what Rani wanted to know. Pratik correctly said that a rocket is used to go to the Moon. Chandra means Moon and yaan means vehicle, so Chandrayaan means the Moon vehicle. India launched Chandrayaan on 14 July 2023 and it landed on the Moon on 23 August 2023. Rani asked if she could go to the Moon too, and Nandini smiled and said maybe, one day. Rani is curious because she asks many questions, and curiosity is how scientists begin.
Curious means eager to learn and know things. Excitement is the feeling of being very happy and thrilled. Machines are things that do work. Confused means not sure what is happening. A scientist is a person who studies and finds out how things work. A rocket is a vehicle that travels very fast into space.
We use a before a singular word that starts with a consonant sound, like a dog, a cow, a sparrow and a girl. We use an before a singular word that starts with a vowel sound, like an eagle, an umbrella, an ice-cream man and an egg. Listen to the sound, not just the letter: an hour starts with a vowel sound, but a university starts with a y sound. Mary ate an apricot, a chikoo and an orange.
Many words start with two letters that make one sound. Sw gives swing and sweet. Sk gives skirt and skate. Sp gives spoon and spin. St gives stone and story. So we say swings in the park, stones in the river, a spoon and a bowl for soup, the story of the boy who cried wolf, and a blue skirt.
There are seven days in a week, and each day has a place in order. Sunday is the first, Monday the second, Tuesday the third and Wednesday the fourth. Thursday is the fifth, Friday the sixth and Saturday the seventh. These position words, first, second, third and so on, are called ordinal numbers.
You can imagine staying on the Moon for ten days and list what you would take, like food, water, a warm suit, a torch and a book. You can draw the Moon and write a few lines about it with your teacher. Collect newspaper clippings about Chandrayaan 3 and make a class chart, and ask your family for a song or story about the Moon in your own language.

problem.en: Fill in a or an: ___ eagle sat on ___ building.

text.en: Eagle starts with a vowel sound, so we use an.
Building starts with a consonant sound, so we use a.
So: An eagle sat on a building.

why.en: Say it aloud to hear the difference.

problem.en: Which day is the fifth day of the week?

text.en: Count from Sunday as first.
The next is Thursday.
